title: 5 Ideas for How Mayor Mamdani Can Bolster Workforce Development
plain_title: Five ideas for strengthening job training in the city
what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City think tank, setting out five proposals for how city government could strengthen job training and expand access to middle-wage careers.
background: The report describes workforce development in the city as an ecosystem spread across many agencies, with roughly 1.1 million working-age New Yorkers unemployed, underemployed or earning the minimum wage.

findings.plain: Entry-level hiring has fallen sharply, making it harder for New Yorkers to get a first foot in the door.
findings.quote: The market for entry-level jobs has plunged 37 percent since 2022

findings.plain: The citywide unemployment rate masks large gaps by race, with Black New Yorkers unemployed at nearly double the overall rate as of December.
findings.quote: an unemployment rate of 9.6 percent for Black New Yorkers as of December

findings.plain: Funding for job programs serving working-age adults has dropped sharply at the two agencies that run much of the system since the Bloomberg administration ended.
findings.quote: down 43.4 percent at the Human Resources Administration (HRA) and 28.4 percent at the Department of Small Business Services (SBS)

findings.plain: The city leans heavily on federal money for job training, which comes with spending limits and caps on cost per participant.
findings.quote: Nearly 40 percent of funding for the city’s core workforce development programs flows from Washington.

findings.plain: Responsibility for workforce development is spread across many agencies and several deputy mayors, which the report says leaves investments siloed and accountability fragmented.
findings.quote: More than 21 city agencies play a role

findings.plain: Everyday costs such as transit fares and childcare, rather than tuition, are what stop many students and trainees from finishing.
findings.quote: Fewer than one in three nonprofit workforce development organizations are able to provide transit subsidies

findings.plain: Career outcomes at the City University of New York (CUNY) lag behind its enrollment gains, and its career success programs reach only a small share of students.
findings.quote: Just two-thirds of CUNY graduates are employed within a year of graduation

recommendations: Make a large new city investment in workforce development through a NYC Talent Development Fund, a $25 million Career Impact Bond, a Workforce AI Readiness Fund with a mayoral task force, and workforce commitments built into neighborhood rezonings.
Appoint a workforce development czar reporting to the mayor and create an Economic Mobility Cabinet in City Hall to coordinate workforce policy and funding across agencies.

Provide free unlimited OMNY cards and childcare support starting on day one to City University of New York (CUNY) undergraduates and participants in workforce training programs, and evaluate the results.

Recruit the next 100 large and mid-sized employers to build skills-based hiring pathways with CUNY and nonprofit training providers, with a goal of 100,000 more hires of lower-income New Yorkers over a decade.

Scale up CUNY's career success programs, including CUNY Beyond, the Inclusive Economy Initiative and CUNY 2X Tech, and set a target that at least 30 percent of students complete a paid internship or work-based learning before graduating.
